title: The Q3 Capex Prints: $730 Billion of 2026 Guides, and What They Do Not Say About Power
description: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon reported the September quarter between October 21 and 29, 2026. Their 2026 capital spending guides now add to about $730 billion. Every number here is read from the release, the 8-K or the call, with the definitional differences spelled out, and the post ends with the figure none of them report: megawatts.
content:
The four largest US buyers of data center capacity reported the September quarter over nine days: Meta on October 21, Microsoft and Alphabet on October 28, Amazon on October 29. GridTilt's capex registry had been sitting on FY2025 guides since May. This post is the refresh, written for a power and grid audience, with each figure taken from the company's own release, 8-K exhibit or earnings call. The sum at the end is ours and is labeled as such.

## What each company said

| Company | Quarter reported | Quarter capex | 2026 guide | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | FY2027 Q1 (Jul to Sep 2026) | $45.2B | about $170B for calendar 2026 | includes $7.4B of finance leases |
| Alphabet | Q3 2026 | $51.4B | $195B to $205B, unchanged | cash purchases of property and equipment |
| Meta | Q3 2026 | $34.91B | $135B to $145B, narrowed from $130B to $145B | includes principal payments on finance leases |
| Amazon | Q3 2026 | $77.3B | about $220B of cash capex, unchanged | purchases of property and equipment, before $1.4B of sale proceeds and incentives |

**Microsoft.** Amy Hood on the October 28 call: "Capital expenditures were $45.2 billion, as some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed." Finance leases were $7.4 billion of that. For the next quarter: "we expect CapEx spend will be over $50 billion." For the year: "for the calendar year, spend should be approximately $170 billion due to the 3P capacity delays noted earlier." The July figure had been about $175 billion. She also said roughly three quarters of the quarter's capex went to short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. Microsoft's fiscal year ends in June, so the $170 billion is a calendar-year estimate, not a fiscal guide.

**Alphabet.** The 8-K exhibit shows purchases of property and equipment of $51,355 million for the quarter. On the call: "our full-year 2026 CapEx guidance range of $195-$205 billion remain unchanged," and "We continue to expect our CapEx to increase significantly in 2027."

**Meta.** From the October 21 release: "Capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, were $34.91 billion." The 2026 outlook is "in the range of $135-145 billion, narrowed from our prior outlook of $130-145 billion." On 2027 the release says only that Meta is "still developing our budget and capacity plans for next year."

**Amazon.** The 8-K exhibit's cash flow statement shows purchases of property and equipment of $77,259 million and proceeds from sales and incentives of $1,381 million for the quarter. The release repeats the full-year line: "We continue to expect 2026 cash capital expenditures to be approximately $220 billion."

## The sum, and why it is directional

Adding the four guides at the midpoints of the two ranges gives about $730 billion for 2026: Microsoft $170 billion, Alphabet $200 billion, Meta $140 billion, Amazon $220 billion. Against the FY2025 guides the registry carried until this week, which summed to $340 billion, that is more than double.

The sum is ours and it mixes four definitions. Microsoft and Meta count finance leases, which means leased buildings and equipment enter capex at the start of the lease. Alphabet and Amazon report cash purchases. Microsoft's number is a calendar-year estimate across two fiscal years. Treat $730 billion as the scale of the thing, not an accounting total.

## What the prints say about power

Capex is a dollar figure. The grid cares about megawatts, and none of the four companies reports them. Three things in the prints still bear on power.

- **Capacity, not cash, was the binding constraint at Microsoft this quarter.** The quarter came in under plan and the year came down by about $5 billion because third-party capacity deliveries slipped. A company that cannot spend its budget on schedule is waiting on buildings, interconnections and equipment, not on money.
- **Most of the spend is servers, not sites.** Microsoft's three-quarters figure for short-lived assets means most of its capex lands inside buildings that already have power. Server refreshes raise the load per rack at an existing site without appearing in any interconnection queue.
- **The 2027 direction is up at two of the four.** Alphabet said significantly higher. Microsoft said spend accelerates in the second half of its fiscal year. Meta has not set a number. Amazon's release does not address 2027.

For scale only: the Compute Frontier page uses Epoch AI's rule of thumb of about $38 billion of capital per gigawatt of IT capacity. At that rate $730 billion would correspond to something under 20 GW if every dollar built new data center capacity. It does not, for the reasons above, so the honest reading is narrower: the money is there, the buildings and the power are what take time. GridTilt tracks 241 named clusters with 130.8 GW of planned power and 15.7 GW energized today; the gap between those two figures is the same gap the capex prints describe from the other side.

## Where this lives on the site

The registry behind this post is at the [Microsoft](/operator/microsoft), [Alphabet](/operator/google), [Meta](/operator/meta) and [Amazon](/operator/amazon) operator pages, each line linked to its filing. The change is logged in the site's [documented changes](/timeline?type=correction).

## Sources

- Microsoft FY27 Q1 earnings call transcript, October 28, 2026: [microsoft.com](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/investor/events/fy-2027/earnings-fy-2027-q1)
- Alphabet Q3 2026 earnings release, 8-K exhibit 99.1, October 28, 2026: [sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001652044/000165204426000080/googexhibit991q32026.htm); Q3 2026 earnings call: [abc.xyz](https://abc.xyz/investor/events/event-details/2026/2026-Q3-Earnings-Call-2026-Ujou16CTw9/default.aspx)
- Meta Q3 2026 earnings release, October 21, 2026: [investor.atmeta.com](https://investor.atmeta.com/investor-news/press-release-details/2026/Meta-Reports-Third-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)
- Amazon Q3 2026 earnings release, 8-K exhibit 99.1, October 29, 2026: [sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001018724/000101872426000038/amzn-20260930xex991.htm)

title: Texas Paused Data Center Energizations. Here Is What ERCOT's Own Deck Says.
description: On August 3, 2026 the Governor directed a verification and audit of every data center in ERCOT's interconnection process, and ERCOT stopped approving new energizations of 75 MW or more. Its September board deck puts numbers on the queue: 204 projects conditionally in as base load, 158 studied, 373 excluded. The reports that decide who stays are due December 10.
content:
Texas has the largest pile of data center interconnection requests in the country and, since August, a pause on energizing them. This post reads the documents ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission have published about it: the August 3 market notice, the September 14 board deck, and the adopted Senate Bill 6 rule as printed in the Texas Register. Every figure is theirs. The one addition is ours and is marked.

## What happened, in order

- **August 3, 2026.** Governor Abbott directed the Commission and ERCOT to complete, in ERCOT's words, "a comprehensive verification and audit" of all data centers advancing through the interconnection process before allowing those loads to proceed. The same day ERCOT issued a market notice pausing the Batch Zero study process and delaying the final classification of all large loads. It also paused approvals to energize data centers and crypto mining facilities of 75 MW or greater.
- **August 10 and 20.** ERCOT asked the Commission for three good cause exceptions to the Batch Zero timelines in its Planning Guide. The Commission granted all three on August 20.
- **September 3.** ERCOT sent each transmission service provider a conditional classification for its large loads: base load, studied load, or excluded, with the reason for any exclusion.
- **September 14 to 15.** ERCOT's board received the Batch Zero update summarized below, for information only.
- **September 18 and October 8.** The Commission's large load interconnection rule, 16 TAC 25.194, was filed with the Secretary of State and took effect three weeks later.
- **December 10.** ERCOT files its Batch Zero Eligibility Verification Report and its Community Impact Review Report with the Commission. Final inclusion follows.

## The numbers in the board deck

Batch Zero is ERCOT's one-time transitional study of large loads that want to connect and meet the eligibility criteria in Planning Guide Revision Request 145. A large load is 75 MW or greater. The deck's conditional classification as of September 3:

| Bucket | Projects | Capacity |
|---|---|---|
| Base load (conditionally included) | 204 | 66.4 GW |
| Studied load (conditionally included) | 158 | 125.4 GW on the eligibility chart; 127.9 GW on the summary slide |
| Excluded | 373 | 302.2 GW |

The two studied-load figures are both in the deck; we show both rather than pick one. Adding ERCOT's three buckets gives roughly 494 GW of requests across 735 projects, our arithmetic on their numbers.

Base load is the firmer bucket. It is made up of load that was energized before or after March 25, 2022, load included in the May 2026 study cycle or earlier, load in the Permian Basin reliability plan, advancing and committed large load under the guide's criteria, and net metering load under PURA 39.169. Studied load is split into firm load, flexible load (PCLR), and load that brings its own generation (WLPUN).

The deck also places the load. Conditional base load for 2032 is heaviest in North Central (14,559 MW) and North (14,222 MW), then Coast (10,976 MW) and Far West (8,493 MW). Studied load for 2032 is 25,807 MW in North Central, 24,309 MW in North, 20,447 MW in South and 16,395 MW in West. The top base load counties are Dallas (5,713 MW), Harris (5,672 MW), Haskell (2,689 MW), Brazoria (2,357 MW) and Ellis (2,330 MW).

Eleven projects in the batch bring their own generation: 9,478 MW of load against 15,444 MW of generation, of which 12,824 MW is gas, 1,654 MW solar, 637 MW wind and 330 MW battery. Nine of the eleven carry more generation than load.

## What the pause does and does not do

The energization pause applies to large load data centers and crypto facilities not yet connected to the ERCOT system. Loads already energized are not affected. ERCOT says the verification and audit and the community impact review are two separate work streams, both on schedule, and that their effect on the Batch Zero study timeline is still to be determined. PGRR 145 originally required ERCOT to finish the study by April 9, 2027.

A developer excluded from Batch Zero can dispute the exclusion through ERCOT's alternative dispute resolution process. A developer reclassified from base to studied load can dispute under Planning Guide section 9.3.1.

## The rule that now governs new requests

The Commission adopted 16 TAC 25.194 under Project 58481 to implement Senate Bill 6. It applies to a large load customer not energized by October 8, 2026 that seeks a new interconnection of 75 MW or more at a single site, certain expansions, or co-location with a generation resource. Before being included in an ERCOT study the customer signs an intermediate agreement, makes required disclosures, and posts financial security of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand. At the standard interconnection agreement the security becomes the greater of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand or the costs allocated to the customer for system upgrades. The preamble leaves transmission cost recovery to a separate rulemaking, Project 58000; Senate Bill 6 requires the Commission to amend its transmission charge rules by December 31, 2026.

## What this means if you live in Texas

Nothing in these documents raises or lowers a residential bill. What they decide is which of roughly 494 GW of requests ERCOT will plan transmission and reserves around, and on what schedule. The December 10 reports are the next real date. GridTilt's [Texas page](/state/texas) carries these documents with their dates and will be updated when the reports land.

## Sources

- ERCOT Board of Directors, Item 14: Batch Zero Update, September 14 to 15, 2026: [ercot.com](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/09/11/14-Batch-Zero-Update.pdf)
- ERCOT Market Notice M-A080326-01, Update Regarding Batch Zero Timelines and Processes, August 3, 2026: [ercot.com](https://www.ercot.com/services/comm/mkt_notices/M-A080326-01)
- Texas Register, October 2, 2026, Adopted Rules, 16 TAC 25.194: [sos.state.tx.us](https://www.sos.state.tx.us/texreg/archive/October22026/Adopted%20Rules/16.ECONOMIC%20REGULATION.html)
- ERCOT, 89th Legislative Session: ERCOT Status, October 2026: [ercot.com](https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/09/15/89th-Legislative-Session-PPTX-ERCOT-Status-October-2026-Final-PDF.pdf)

title: Anthropic's S-1: The Compute Bill, the Power Risk, and What the Filing Leaves Out
description: Anthropic filed to go public on October 26, 2026. The prospectus discloses more than $630 billion of named compute commitments, a first operating profit, and a data center strategy that now includes on-site gas generation. It discloses no megawatts.
content:
Anthropic, PBC filed its Form S-1 with the SEC on October 26, 2026, to list Class A shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT. The filing is preliminary: the price range, the offering size, the third-quarter financials and the headline total of committed spend are all left blank. What it does contain is the most detailed public account so far of how one frontier lab buys compute, where it plans to put it, and what it thinks can go wrong with the power.

This post reads the filing for a power and data center audience. Every figure below comes from the prospectus itself, by section, and the derived numbers are marked as ours. The document is at [sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002130357/000162828026067168/anthropicpbc-sx1.htm).

## The numbers the filing does report

The income statement covers fiscal 2023 through 2025, the six months ended June 30 of 2025 and 2026, and six quarters from the first quarter of 2025 through the second quarter of 2026. Operating metrics are given as of September 30, 2026. Third-quarter dollar figures are blank.

| Period | Revenue | Compute and infrastructure | Operating income (loss) | Net loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | $386M | $2,522M | $(2,980)M | $(8,309)M |
| FY2025 | $4,585M | $7,326M | $(8,060)M | $(41,965)M |
| Q1 2026 | $4,731M | $3,387M | $(1,667)M | $(14,439)M |
| Q2 2026 | $11,555M | $5,558M | $974M | $(66,309)M |
| H1 2026 | $16,286M | $8,945M | $(693)M | $(80,748)M |

Three things stand out.

- The second quarter of 2026 was the first with an operating profit. The filing attributes it to revenue growing faster than operating expenses. Revenue grew 1,368% year over year in that quarter while compute and infrastructure expense grew 300%.
- The net losses are almost entirely accounting marks on convertible notes. The change in fair value of convertible notes, derivatives and SAFEs was $72.4 billion in the first half of 2026. Operating cash flow in the same half was positive $3.9 billion. Cash and cash equivalents were $112.4 billion and short-term investments $19.3 billion at June 30, 2026.
- Compute and infrastructure expense fell from 251% of revenue in the first quarter of 2025 to 48% in the second quarter of 2026. The company says most of its compute is contracted 12 to 18 months ahead, and that it expects to buy more short-term compute near term, which "typically carries a higher cost per unit of compute" and will compress operating margin.

Capital expenditure is still small on the balance sheet. Purchases of property and equipment were $131 million in fiscal 2025 and $482 million in the first half of 2026. The filing says capital expenditures will "increase significantly" as the build-out expands. Most of the compute spending runs through leases and cloud contracts, which is where the large numbers sit.

## The compute bill, counterparty by counterparty

The filing's own aggregate figure is blank. What it discloses are the individual agreements, in the Contractual Obligations section, and three dated subtotals in the notes.

| Counterparty | Commitment | Term | Cancellable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google (cloud and TPUs) | at least about $114.5B, take-or-pay with a true-up | April 2026 to July 2033 | No, except Google's uncured material breach |
| Google and other TPU providers, additional capacity | estimated $125B to $150B, not in the commitments table | delivered 2028 to 2031 | Terms not final |
| Amazon | at least $110.0B, take-or-pay with a true-up | May 2026 to April 2036 | No, except Amazon's uncured material breach |
| Broadcom equipment leases (TPU-based systems) | about $161.2B of rent excluding interest, finance leases | five-year leases; capacity from 2026, more from 2027 | No, except default |
| SpaceX.AI (formerly X.AI), NVIDIA GPUs | up to $120.5B; about $3.1B per month once fully delivered, expected December 2026 | into 2029 | Non-cancellable periods end January and March 2027; then either party on 90 days' notice |
| Microsoft | at least $44.9B "regardless of actual usage" | November 2026 to May 2033 | No, except breach or per undelivered tranche |
| Nscale, NVIDIA GPUs | up to about $44.6B, fees as capacity is delivered and accepted | into 2033 | Limited; Nscale must secure financing and meet delivery requirements |
| Lambda, NVIDIA GPUs | about $41.3B; $34.9B of it in an August 2026 agreement | into 2034 | The August agreement can be terminated by either party if Lambda does not secure its facility lease |
| AMD (Helios rack-scale systems, MI450 series) | no fixed dollar amount; more than $20B if the full initial tranche is taken, with an option for about as much again | first tranche in calendar 2027 | Not by Anthropic, except AMD's uncured breach |

Summing the named counterparties gives about $637 billion of commitments with a stated dollar amount. Adding the AMD floor and the additional TPU estimate takes the figure to roughly $780 billion to $810 billion. That sum is our arithmetic, not a filing total, and it is not all firm: the SpaceX.AI arrangement becomes cancellable in early 2027, and the Nscale and Lambda agreements carry outs tied to financing and facility leases.

The notes give three subtotals that corroborate the scale. Non-cancellable purchase commitments were $54.6 billion at December 31, 2025. Expected fixed or minimum guaranteed commitments were about $265.6 billion at June 30, 2026, with terms from one to 20 years. Between July 1 and October 26, 2026, the company added about $245 billion more in minimum payment obligations, plus about $21 billion of short-term non-cancellable contracts. Commitments run as far as 2045.

Part of this capacity is financed by the sellers. The filing lists note purchase agreements under which Google may fund up to $20 billion, Amazon up to $15 billion in $5 billion increments tied to compute capacity milestones, and Broadcom up to $42 billion, the last "solely to finance quarterly rent obligations" under the 2026 lease arrangement at 9% paid in kind. The filing states that "a portion of our compute and infrastructure build-out has been funded or supported by capital or credit support provided or facilitated by certain of our CSPs and chip partners," and that some financing arrangements require exclusive or preferential supply commitments with particular chip suppliers.

## Anthropic Direct: leased chips in leased buildings

The filing names the company's data center strategy "Anthropic Direct." In its words: "we also procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification." The first such facility "became operational this year."

The structure separates the building from the chips on purpose. "Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain."

The pieces the filing describes:

- Accelerators, CPUs and high-bandwidth memory come through master equipment leases with Broadcom, deployed in facilities "operated by others on our behalf." The leases are accounted for as finance leases and rent starts when equipment is ready for service, or earlier if a facility is delayed.
- Buildings come through partners who "procure the underlying real estate, power, and data center facilities," with Anthropic leasing capacity and contracting operators. A colocation and services agreement with Fluidstack USA I Inc. covers data center development and operations. The company has also "executed data center leases directly and expect to do so increasingly over time." One subsequent event is a lease signed in March 2026 "for a data center to be constructed," commencing in 2027 for a term of 20 years.
- Some development projects depend on partners who guarantee the lease obligations for capacity that will host that partner's chips. The risk factors add that some arrangements "depend on the continued performance of credit support provided by a third party that is also a competitor."
- Power "requires separate arrangements with utility providers or, in some cases, development of behind-the-meter power generation capacity that supplies electricity directly to the facility rather than through the broader electric grid."

The projects are "currently located primarily in the United States," with international capacity being pursued and letters of intent signed in "multiple non-U.S. jurisdictions." Long-lived assets were 95% in the U.S. at June 30, 2026.

## What the filing says about power

The power section is the part of this document most relevant to the buildout GridTilt tracks, and it is more specific than the rest of the filing.

On-site gas is in the plan. "Certain of our planned data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation, which exposes us to fuel price volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control and for which we bear the cost on a pass-through basis." The arrangements "generally provide for fuel and related costs to be borne by us on a pass-through basis without cost caps." The filing expects "increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity" where behind-the-meter generation is allowed, and names pipeline capacity, firm transportation and laterals as constraints that could delay or end a site.

Some contracts are 20 years long and pay regardless of use. "Certain of our dedicated power and data center infrastructure arrangements have initial terms of 20 years with annual escalators and include take-or-pay compute payment obligations and uncapped fuel cost pass-throughs that apply for the duration of the term regardless of actual utilization." The company may also "enter into arrangements involving dedicated power generation assets and/or the development, operation, or control of power stations or other energy infrastructure." A subsequent event records a guaranty of up to $500 million backing a provider's power purchase contract at a U.S. facility.

The grid is described as the constraint. "The availability of sufficient electrical power has emerged as a significant constraint on data center development and expansion in many geographies, including the United States." Interconnection queues "have also lengthened substantially in many regions." Utilities may require the company "to bear grid upgrade or interconnection costs beyond those attributable to serving our facilities." High-voltage transformers, switchgear, turbines, generators and substations face "extended delivery timelines, price increases, tariffs and national security requirements, and allocation constraints," and the company may pay above market for long-lead equipment to pull capacity forward.

Moratoriums are named as a live risk. "Certain state, local, and municipal jurisdictions in the United States are also considering or have approved moratoriums on new data center construction." The two examples given are New York, which has paused state permitting for new large facilities, and Texas, which subjects large loads "to curtailment or disconnection during grid emergencies." The filing adds that "opposition to data center development has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us."

The ratepayer pledge is now a disclosed cost. "We have publicly committed to covering the cost of electricity price increases to consumers caused by our data centers, including both the cost of electricity itself and the infrastructure necessary to deliver it." The company also lists voluntary commitments to cover grid upgrade costs, procure new generation to match its load, and invest in curtailment systems, and says these commitments "have increased, and we expect will continue to increase, our operating costs."

Water gets one sentence: facilities "depend on access to reliable water for cooling, which in some regions is scarce, subject to use restrictions, or increasingly costly."

## What is not in the filing

For a document this long, the physical disclosures are thin. A search of the full text finds:

- No megawatt or gigawatt figure anywhere, for any facility, contract or plan.
- No named Anthropic data center site, city or state. New York and Texas appear only as regulatory examples.
- No chip counts, and no named TPU or Trainium generation. NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems and AMD MI450 are named as platforms.
- No power usage effectiveness, emissions, renewable share, water volume or electricity spend. Electricity appears only inside the definition of compute and infrastructure expense, as "committed power costs associated with our data center operations."
- No mention of Oracle, CoreWeave, Crusoe, or the "$50 billion" U.S. data center plan reported in the press. The only "50 billion" in the text is inside the "$125 billion to $150 billion" TPU estimate.
- No third-quarter financials, no aggregate committed-spend total, and an empty contractual obligations table.

Several of these blanks are normal for a first public filing and will be filled in amendments. The absence of any capacity figure is still notable: the company describes a strategy of leasing buildings and power years ahead of the chips, and discloses hundreds of billions in payment obligations, without stating how much load that represents.

## Reading it against the buildout

A few conclusions follow for anyone tracking data centers and the grid.

The hyperscaler contracts are demand that has already been booked into other companies' capital plans. Google ($114.5 billion), Amazon ($110 billion) and Microsoft ($44.9 billion) are selling capacity they must build and power. Those dollars show up as hyperscaler capex and as interconnection requests, whoever the end customer is.

The neocloud and chip-partner contracts are the newer channel, and they come with their own facilities. Nscale, Lambda and SpaceX.AI are each committing to stand up GPU capacity for a single customer, and the Lambda agreement is explicitly contingent on a facility lease. The Broadcom leases put about $161 billion of TPU-based equipment into buildings run by third parties. This is capacity that will appear on project maps under names other than Anthropic.

On-site gas with uncapped fuel pass-through means a frontier lab now carries direct exposure to Henry Hub and to pipeline capacity in specific basins. The filing names that exposure and the competition for it. It is the same constraint showing up in the behind-the-meter projects already on the Power Map.

The regulatory examples are current. New York's permitting pause and Texas's curtailment rules for large loads are both named in a federal filing as risks to a company's ability to build. Expect other states' actions to appear in the next amendment.

Finally, the ratepayer pledge has moved from a press statement to an SEC-disclosed operating cost. Whether and how it is honored is now something a public company has to report on.

The next amendment should fill in the third quarter, the aggregate commitment total and the offering size. A capacity figure would allow the commitments to be read in megawatts. Until then the filing gives dollars and years only.

Source: Anthropic, PBC, Form S-1, filed October 26, 2026 (sections cited: Summary Consolidated Financial and Other Data; Risk Factors, "Electrical Power and Fuel Constraints" and "Data Center Infrastructure"; Management's Discussion and Analysis, "Contractual Obligations"; Business, "Our Data Center Strategy"; Notes 13, 16 and 17). This is analysis of a public filing, not investment advice.

title: The Data Center Panic Does Not Add Up: Bills, Water and the Grid
description: Most Americans say they do not want a data center nearby. The published numbers on electric rates, water use and grid investment point the other way, with one real exception: the result depends on whether the power system can keep up.
content:
Roughly 70% of Americans say they do not want a data center built near them, according to survey evidence cited by Watten, Bistline and Blanford (2026). The reasons are easy to state. A data center is a large building full of servers running all day and all night. The immediate fears are that it will raise the electric bill, strain the grid and drain the local water supply. State legislatures of both parties are debating restrictions, and towns are passing moratoriums every month.

Those concerns are reasonable. The published numbers do not support most of them. On the evidence available in October 2026, data center growth has coincided with slightly lower average residential rates, data centers use a small share of national water, and the grid upgrades they pay for stay in the community. The one argument that does hold is about supply: if demand grows faster than generation and transmission can be built, the effect reverses.

A note on perspective: the author works in electrical distribution, marketing lighting and electrical gear to contractors, including supplies for data center work, and builds GridTilt to track how power moves through the grid. That is the vantage point for what follows.

## Electric bills

The intuition is straightforward. A data center is a giant new customer, giant customers use a lot of power, and more demand should mean higher prices.

A 2026 paper by Asa Watten, John Bistline and Geoffrey Blanford, "Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States," found the opposite over the period it studied. Looking at data center growth from 2019 to 2024, the authors estimate that each 10% increase in data center capacity was associated with a roughly 0.4% decline in average residential prices. In the areas where capacity grew about 160%, rates were about 6% lower than they would otherwise have been. A separate evaluation of that paper, including its limitations, is [here](/blog/study-data-centers-electricity-rates).

The mechanism is fixed costs. A utility pays for transmission lines, substations and transformers whether or not anyone uses them, and every kilowatt-hour sold carries a share of that cost. A large new customer spreads the fixed cost over more sales, and the price per kilowatt-hour falls. The paper finds this pattern of economies of scale across transmission, distribution and generation costs.

There is a second layer. Utilities are regulated monopolies that earn a set return on the infrastructure they build. When a data center arrives, the utility builds new substations and heavy-duty lines to serve it, and the data center pays for that construction through connection fees and monthly bills. Once the lines are in the ground they belong to the local grid. The utility earns its regulated return, the data center pays, and the neighborhood ends up with a stronger grid than it had.

Virginia is the test case. It has the most data centers in the country, using over 20% of the state's electricity, and its rate increases have tracked the national average. California is often raised as a counterexample, with prices up about 40%, but most of that increase traces to wildfire-related costs rather than data centers. Nationally from 2021 to 2024, demand grew about 1.5% a year while rates grew 5.2% a year against inflation of 5.8%, so real rates were roughly flat. All of these figures are from Watten et al.

## Water

Water is easier to measure. The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (Shehabi et al.) estimates that U.S. data centers used about 17.4 billion gallons of water for cooling in 2023.

That is a large number in isolation and a small one in context. Axios's compilation of national water use by sector puts data centers at about 627 million gallons a day, against about 137 billion gallons a day for cattle, 133 billion for power plants and 23.3 billion for residential use. Even adding the water used at power plants to generate the electricity data centers consume, the combined footprint is a small fraction of national use. Agriculture accounts for 70% to 80% of withdrawals in arid states (Dhanasekar, Smart Water Magazine).

Location matters more than the national total. A facility in a dry county will use water, and a single site can consume the equivalent of a few thousand households. It is rarely the primary driver of regional scarcity next to agriculture.

The engineering is also moving. Microsoft has announced a data center design that uses almost no water for cooling: the loop is filled once at construction and recirculates between servers and chillers without evaporating, at the cost of somewhat more electricity. The company estimates the design saves more than 33 million gallons per data center per year (Construction Executive). Newer hyperscale facilities are adopting closed-loop, direct-to-chip liquid cooling that recirculates water without evaporation (Dhanasekar). The high-water facilities are the older ones using cheap evaporative cooling, and the industry is moving away from that design. The policy that follows is to require the newer cooling technology in new permits.

## The benefits that go uncounted

New technologies draw opposition before their uses are clear. The pattern repeats with the printing press, the telephone and the internet, and the benefits look obvious only in hindsight.

Electricity has its own version of this history. Watten et al. note that in the second half of the 20th century, U.S. electricity demand rose while real prices fell. Demand growth and price growth are not the same thing.

Two benefits in particular go unmentioned at hearings. The first is the money that stays in ratepayers' pockets when fixed costs are spread more widely. The second is the infrastructure itself. A data center may pay for a new substation or new transmission lines, and that equipment stays for decades after the servers are replaced. It can serve future housing, and it can provide backup capacity for hospitals. The data center pays the upfront cost and the community keeps the asset.

Entergy Mississippi offers a current example. In September 2025 the utility proposed an additional $300 million of grid reliability spending, on top of $600 million already committed, with a target of cutting outage frequency and duration for the average customer by 50% within five years. Entergy says the added spending will be funded by revenue from Amazon and other large new customers rather than by rate increases, subject to approval by the Mississippi Public Service Commission ([Entergy](https://www.entergy.com/blog/entergy-mississippi-is-powering-up-the-grid-to-save-customers-2-billion)).

## The argument that holds

The skeptics' strongest point is about supply, and the Watten paper makes it explicitly: "future supply constraints could reverse the effect." If data centers add load faster than generation and transmission can be built, utilities run their oldest and most expensive plants and buy scarce power at high prices, and the extra demand raises costs instead of spreading them.

This is a real engineering constraint. A gigawatt-scale campus cannot be built in two years if the transmission lines take ten years to permit and build. The transformer supply chain is backed up and there are waiting lists for basic grid equipment. A utility caught flat-footed will buy spot-market power at peak prices, and its ratepayers will see it on their bills. The paper does not claim its result is permanent; it says the result depends on the power system keeping up with demand.

The skeptics are therefore not saying data centers are a bad deal. They are saying the outcome depends on whether the grid can keep up. That is a problem with the grid's capacity to build, and the response is to build supply rather than ban demand. In March 2026 the White House secured a pledge from seven major technology companies to pay for their own grid upgrades (as reported in Watten et al.). Banning the data center does not fix the grid; it leaves the same fixed costs spread across fewer customers, which is the scenario that raises rates. The approach a number of utility and grid experts favor is to make the data center pay for its own interconnection and its own generation, which is what the pledge is meant to do.

## Conclusion

On bills, the measured effect in the high-density states has been flat to slightly lower rates. On water, the sector's use is small next to agriculture and power generation, and the newest facilities are designed to use almost none. On the grid, the upgrades a data center pays for remain in place for the community. The risk that remains is a supply constraint, and it argues for building generation and transmission faster, with the developer paying, rather than for moratoriums. More data centers are coming as more of daily life moves onto digital services. The decisions about where and how to build them should rest on the numbers.

Sources: [Watten, Bistline and Blanford, "Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States," arXiv, June 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19777); [Shehabi et al., 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, LBNL](https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/lbnl-2024-united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report_1.pdf); [Axios, "Estimated U.S. water use, select industries," June 2026](https://graphics.axios.com/hermesv2/2026-06-24-911-data-center-water/index.html); [Construction Executive, "Dry Data: Zero-Water Data Center Design," February 2026](https://constructionexec.com/article/dry-data/); [Dhanasekar, "Reframing the Narrative: Contextualizing Data Center Water Use," Smart Water Magazine, February 2026](https://smartwatermagazine.com/blogs/ashwin-dhanasekar/reframing-narrative-contextualizing-data-center-water-use).

title: CXMT's 4F² DRAM Cell: What It Changes and What It Does Not
description: CXMT announced a vertical-transistor DRAM cell that cuts cell area by a third without EUV. On the numbers it lands roughly even with Micron's current EUV node, it has not been made at volume by anyone, and CXMT's supply is limited by wafers. It is a 2028 to 2030 risk for the industry, not a Q4 problem for Micron.
content:
On October 10, 2026, CXMT said its first 4F² DRAM would be a DDR5 server RDIMM due by the end of the year. Samsung and SK hynix each fell about 7% on the news, and Sandisk sold off with them despite not making DRAM. This note explains what the cell is and why it does not change the near-term picture for Micron. The companion piece on Micron's price target is [here](/blog/micron-bear-case-12-month-target).

## What 4F² means

A DRAM cell's footprint is measured in units of F, the minimum feature size of the process. Every cell shipped today is 6F²: the access transistor lies flat, so each cell occupies about 3F by 2F. A 4F² cell stands the transistor up vertically and wraps the gate around a thin silicon pillar, so the cell shrinks to 2F by 2F. That is about a third less area per cell on paper.

For a company that cannot buy EUV lithography tools, this is the available route to density. If the process cannot print smaller features, the cell layout is what is left to change. Samsung, SK hynix and Micron all have 4F² on their own roadmaps for the point at which they need it.

## Why it is not a near-term problem for Micron

- The cell size ends up about even with what Micron already ships. Cell area is the layout factor times F². CXMT's most advanced node is roughly 16nm-class without EUV; Micron's 1-gamma node uses EUV at roughly 13nm-class. In round numbers, 4 x 16² is about 1,020 nm² and 6 x 13² is about 1,010 nm². A perfect 4F² implementation puts CXMT at parity with Micron's current cell, not ahead of it.
- No one has made it at volume. The bitline is buried under the transistor, the gate wraps a tall narrow pillar, and the capacitor has to land on top of that pillar. Tighter spacing worsens row hammer, the pillar traps charge in ways a planar transistor does not, and the deep etches have little margin. CXMT announced no speeds, capacities, yields or customer qualifications, and Korean press reported the first parts may use the new cell only partly. New cell designs have historically needed four to eight quarters to yield profitably.
- Supply is limited by wafers, not cells. CXMT runs roughly 320,000 to 350,000 wafers a month against Micron's roughly 385,000, and its next fabs arrive in 2028 or later. A denser cell raises bits per wafer, but output is still bounded by wafer starts. CXMT is also moving wafers into HBM, from about 30,000 to 100,000 starts a month by 2028, and HBM uses about three times the wafer area per bit, which takes supply out of commodity DRAM in the near term.
- Micron has little direct exposure. It has been largely out of Chinese critical infrastructure since 2023, and China is a single-digit share of its fiscal 2027 sales guide. The indirect risk is Samsung and SK hynix supply displaced from China and sold elsewhere, which matters once the shortage ends. CXMT is also about two generations behind on HBM, where Micron is co-designing custom parts with Nvidia.

## What it is

It is a credible route around the EUV restriction and a real risk to DRAM supply in 2028 to 2030, for the industry as a whole rather than for Micron specifically. It does not move volume in the fourth quarter of 2026. Samsung's and SK hynix's 7% declines, and Sandisk's selloff alongside them, read as profit-taking after a large run.

Sources: [Tom's Hardware, CXMT's first 4F² DRAM](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/cxmt-president-says-companys-first-4f2-dram-will-be-a-server-ddr5-rdimm-due-by-year-end-vertical-transistors-cut-each-memory-cells-footprint-by-a-third-on-paper-but-no-speeds-or-capacities-yet); [TweakTown, CXMT 4F² timeline vs Samsung](https://www.tweaktown.com/news/114025/cxmt-plans-to-launch-4f2-ddr5-server-memory-by-year-end-potentially-beating-samsung-by-two-years/index.html); [Tom's Hardware, CXMT capacity near Micron](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/cxmt-close-to-matching-microns-memory-capacity-in-2026-research-claims-would-put-china-on-track-to-become-worlds-second-largest-dram-producer); [EE Times Asia, CXMT's rise](https://www.eetasia.com/cxmts-rise-chinas-memory-champion-challenging-global-leaders/). This is analysis, not investment advice.

title: Micron: Answering the Bear Case and a 12-Month Target of $1,180
description: The three catalysts the bear case says will break in Q4 (a faster CXMT ramp, memory-saving model architectures, and a shift to the edge) are 2028 risks, not Q4 ones. The contracts are take-or-pay with cash down. Probability-weighted target $1,180, range $730 to $1,550.
content:
Micron (MU) closed at $953 on October 13, 2026, down from $1,065 at the end of September and a high near $1,255 during the summer. The bear case making the rounds says one of three things breaks in the fourth quarter: CXMT improves yields and ramps faster than expected, a frontier lab ships an architecture that cuts memory use, or demand slides to the edge through smaller models or hard-coded ASICs. Any of these, the argument goes, calls into question projections built on MOUs and long-term agreements that customers can walk away from.

This post takes those points one at a time. The conclusion is a 12-month target of about $1,180, with a range of $730 to $1,550. The bear case is right about the slowing rate of price increases and half right about the contracts. It is wrong about the timing of everything else.

## CXMT: the risk is capacity in 2028, not a cell design in Q4

On October 10 CXMT announced a 4F² DDR5 server module with a vertical transistor, due "by year-end." The announcement gave no speeds, capacities, yields or customer qualifications, and Korean press reported that the first parts may only partly use the new cell. New DRAM cell structures have historically taken four to eight quarters to reach profitable yield. A technical note on why the 4F² cell does not change Micron's position is [here](/blog/cxmt-4f2-dram-micron).

The real CXMT exposure is wafer capacity that already exists. Counterpoint and SemiAnalysis estimates put CXMT at roughly 320,000 to 350,000 wafers a month today against about 385,000 for Micron, rising toward 500,000 by the end of 2028. That is a supply story for 2028 and later, when CXMT's new fabs land.

Micron is the least directly exposed of the three majors. It has been largely out of Chinese critical infrastructure since 2023 and guides China to a single-digit share of fiscal 2027 sales. The indirect effect is that CXMT displaces Samsung and SK hynix inside China, and that displaced supply has to sell somewhere else. That only hurts once the shortage ends.

One offsetting detail: CXMT is moving wafers into HBM, from about 30,000 to 100,000 wafer starts a month by 2028 on SemiAnalysis's projection. HBM uses roughly three times the wafer area per bit, so those starts come out of commodity DRAM supply and tighten it in the near term.

## Memory-saving architectures: the test has already been run

In March 2026 Google published TurboQuant, claiming about 6x compression of the KV cache. Micron fell about 7% and memory stocks lost roughly $100 billion of market value in a week. Over the following six months DRAM contract prices kept rising and Micron ran to $1,255.

Compression has been part of the whole cycle. DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention has delivered 7x to 14x KV-cache compression since 2024, and FP8 caches are standard. Bit demand grew anyway. Freed capacity goes to longer context windows, more concurrent users and agent workloads. Mixture-of-experts models raise resident memory requirements because every expert's weights stay loaded.

HBM per accelerator is fixed at design time, years ahead. Nvidia sets the HBM capacity of each GPU generation, and Micron has said the vast majority of its calendar 2027 HBM is already contracted at higher prices. A paper published this quarter does not change a 2027 bill of materials.

The concession: TrendForce estimates memory rising from 47% to about 68% of major cloud capex in 2027. When one input is two-thirds of the budget, every hyperscaler has a strong incentive to engineer it out. That is the bear point worth taking seriously, and it is an argument about demand elasticity in 2028 and beyond.

## The edge: still DRAM, and robots do not move the total

Small models on phones and PCs run on DRAM. That is LPDDR, which Micron's mobile and client segment sold at a 90% gross margin last quarter, above HBM's 83%. A shift to the edge changes the product mix. It does not reduce the number of bits. The edge problem Micron actually has today runs the other way: mobile and client bit shipments have fallen two quarters in a row because memory is too expensive for those customers.

Hard-coded ASICs are a niche. Taalas's HC1 hard-wires Llama 3.1 8B into an 815 mm² 6nm die drawing about 2.5 kW at the server level, and the model can never be updated. Humanoid robots retrain their vision-language-action models continuously, so baked-in weights fit them poorly.

Robots are immaterial either way. Counterpoint's estimates for humanoid DRAM:

| Year | DRAM per robot | Total humanoid DRAM | Implied units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 19 GB | about 1 PB | about 55,000 |
| 2030 | 39 GB | about 21.5 PB | about 550,000 |

Global DRAM output runs to tens of exabytes a year, so humanoids are under 0.1% of bits even in 2030. Micron's "200 GB per robot" figure was an autonomous-vehicle number. Robotics belongs in neither the bull case nor the bear case.

## The contracts: half right

Where the bear is right:

- Micron's $134 billion of remaining performance obligations is valued at floor prices on committed volumes. Only $33.5 billion lands in the next 12 months, about 12% of fiscal 2027 consensus revenue. The contracts do not lock in fiscal 2027.
- Customer deposits of $12.75 billion plus $7 billion of letters of credit cover about 15% of the RPO. None of these agreements has been tested in a downturn.

Where the bear is wrong:

- These are take-or-pay Strategic Customer Agreements with cash deposits, not MOUs. The MOU headlines belong to arrangements like the OpenAI wafer letters of intent with Samsung and SK hynix.
- A customer walks away only when market prices fall below the contract floor, which requires a demand collapse first. Abandonment would be a consequence of a downturn, not its cause, and walking costs the deposit and supply priority in a sold-out market.
- Ten of the 26 agreements were signed last quarter at higher prices, and two now run to 2031.

Nothing in the fourth quarter breaks the fundamentals. TrendForce's September 30 outlook has Q4 DRAM contract prices up 10% to 15% and NAND up 15% to 20%. Micron's September-to-November quarter guide of $61.5 billion of revenue and $38.15 of EPS is largely locked.

The real bear signal is deceleration. The fourth-quarter increase is smaller than the third quarter's, and TrendForce says the pace is slowing. Memory stocks have historically peaked two to three quarters before prices do, once the rate of increase starts to fall. That is why Micron trades near 5.5x forward earnings, and why "it is cheap at 5x" is not a complete argument.

## The target

By October 2027 the market will be pricing fiscal 2028 earnings and deciding how far fiscal 2029 falls.

| Case | Probability | What happens | FY2028 EPS | Multiple plus cash | Value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 30% | Shortage lasts through calendar 2027; HBM4 and custom HBM wins; prices ease only in the second half of 2028 | about $215 | 7x plus about $50 | $1,550 |
| Base | 45% | Contract prices peak mid-2027; a Bernstein-style 50% decline in 2028; contract floors cushion Micron | about $185 | 6x plus about $80 | $1,190 |
| Bear | 25% | 2027 hyperscaler capex digestion, the CXMT ramp and efficiency gains arrive together; prices roll over in the second half of 2027 | about $110 | 6x plus about $70 | $730 |

The cash column is net cash and free cash flow accumulated over the year after buybacks. The probability-weighted value is about $1,180, roughly 25% above the October 13 close, with the bear case about 22% below it.

What would change the view, in order:

1. Hyperscaler third-quarter calls in late October, the first 2027 capex signals. Amazon has already said 2027 will be capacity-short.
2. DDR5 spot falling below contract, the earliest warning, months before it shows in Micron's numbers.
3. CXMT's 4F² module being qualified at Alibaba or ByteDance. Qualification at a customer, rather than the launch itself, is the event to watch.
4. Micron's December quarter and the pace of the buyback starting December 9.
5. Taiwan labor: whether the Taoyuan strike happens and whether the 15% profit-share demand holds.

Several figures above come from secondary coverage (Bernstein's 2028 numbers, the CXMT capacity estimates), and sources disagree on some of them. This is analysis, not personalized investment advice.

Sources: [TrendForce, Q4 2026 contract price outlook](https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260930-13258.html); [CNBC, Micron fiscal Q4 2026 results](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/30/micron-mu-q4-earnings-report-2026.html); [Tom's Hardware, CXMT 4F² DDR5 RDIMM](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/cxmt-president-says-companys-first-4f2-dram-will-be-a-server-ddr5-rdimm-due-by-year-end-vertical-transistors-cut-each-memory-cells-footprint-by-a-third-on-paper-but-no-speeds-or-capacities-yet); [Tom's Hardware, CXMT capacity vs Micron](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/cxmt-close-to-matching-microns-memory-capacity-in-2026-research-claims-would-put-china-on-track-to-become-worlds-second-largest-dram-producer); [CNBC, TurboQuant and memory stocks](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/26/google-ai-turboquant-memory-chip-stocks-samsung-micron.html); [Korea JoongAng Daily, humanoid memory demand](https://www.koreajoongangdaily.com/business/humanoid-robots-eyed-as-next-driver-of-memory-chip-demand/12915302); [PC Gamer, Bernstein 2028 forecast](https://www.pcgamer.com/hardware/memory/analysts-think-sk-hynixs-dram-and-nand-prices-will-finally-drop-by-the-end-of-2028-but-not-before-a-huge-rise-over-the-next-year/); [TMT Finance, 2026 hyperscaler capex](https://www.tmtfinance.com/intel/2026-hyperscaler-capex-tops-us700bn-analysis).

title: Reading the Study That Found Data Centers Lowered Electric Rates
description: A June 2026 paper by Watten, Bistline and Blanford finds that data center growth from 2015 to 2024 was associated with slightly lower retail electricity rates. What the paper measures, where its data comes from, who funded it, and the caveat the authors put in their own abstract.
content:
Much of the public conversation about AI data centers concerns electric bills, grid strain and water. One paper addresses the first of those directly: "Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States," by Asa Watten, John Bistline and Geoffrey Blanford, posted to arXiv in June 2026 ([arxiv.org/abs/2606.19777](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19777)). Its headline finding is that data center growth between 2015 and 2024 was associated with slightly lower retail electricity rates. This post evaluates the source: who wrote it, where it was published, what data it uses, where bias could enter, and what the authors themselves say about the limits of the result. The argument that builds on it is [here](/blog/data-center-fears-bills-water-grid).

## The authors

All three authors have backgrounds in energy economics rather than in AI. John Bistline and Geoffrey Blanford hold PhDs from Stanford and have contributed to reports for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change; Bistline also contributed to the Fifth National Climate Assessment. Asa Watten holds a PhD from Michigan State University and was a postdoctoral researcher at Yale and a fellow at the EPA. The topic sits inside work they have done for years, which supports the paper's credibility. Two of the three authors have worked at the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI), which is the main thing to weigh when considering bias, and it is addressed below.

## The venue

The paper is on arXiv, operated by Cornell University and a standard preprint server for physics, mathematics, economics and related fields. Papers on arXiv are not necessarily peer reviewed, and that matters for a paper making a causal claim. It does not disqualify the work. Research about AI infrastructure dates quickly, and a long review process can leave results behind the facts by the time they appear. The authors' backgrounds, the amount of data shown, and the fact that the methods and sources are published for inspection offset the absence of review to a reasonable degree. The paper should still be read as a preprint.

## The title and the abstract

The title is a neutral question followed by a method, "Causal Evidence from the United States," which signals that the paper attempts to separate the effect of data centers from everything else that moved rates over the same period, rather than reporting a simple correlation between data center growth and price changes.

The abstract does not present the finding as permanent. The main result is that data center growth from 2015 to 2024 was associated with slightly lower retail rates. The authors add: "We caution that future supply constraints could reverse the effect." The logic is that if data centers add demand faster than the grid can add generation and transmission, utilities have to run their oldest and most expensive plants and buy scarce power at high prices, and the extra load raises costs instead of spreading them. The result therefore depends on the power system being able to keep up with demand.

## The data

The electricity data come largely from government sources: retail sales and revenue from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and supporting data from FERC, the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The data center capacity series comes from S&P Global Market Intelligence, a private source, so the capacity side of the analysis is harder for outsiders to verify than the price side.

The reference list is long and spans decades. One of the oldest citations is a 1949 statistics paper by Anderson and Rubin, which indicates the authors are using established econometric methods rather than inventing a procedure to reach a preferred answer. The paper also gives historical context for its result: "In the second half of the 20th century, US electricity demand increased while real prices decreased." The argument is that higher electricity demand does not automatically mean higher prices, because utilities can spread fixed costs across more sales.

## Where bias could enter

EPRI conducts research on the electric power industry and is closely connected to utilities. Utilities benefit when electricity demand grows, so there is an obvious reason to scrutinize research concluding that large new loads are not hurting customers, and two of the three authors have EPRI affiliations. That connection does not make the research wrong, but it belongs in any reading of the conclusion.

Several features of the paper reduce the concern. The authors state the limits of their own result, model the supply-constraint case in which the effect reverses, and discuss infrastructure costs, transformer shortages, and the possibility of overbuilding if projected data center demand fails to arrive. They do not claim that data centers always lower rates. They claim that over the period studied, rates did not rise because of them and may have fallen slightly. Because most of the electricity data are federal, other researchers can rerun the analysis and challenge it. The private S&P Global data are the exception.

## What the evaluation shows

The paper is a credible, preprint-stage piece of applied econometrics from authors with relevant track records, using mostly public data and standard methods, with an industry affiliation that warrants attention and a clearly stated boundary on its own conclusion. The title and abstract alone would have been enough to accept it quickly; reading the funding, the data sources and the authors' stated limitations is what makes the finding usable. The headline is that data centers may have lowered rates. The paper's explanation is economies of scale and the spreading of fixed grid costs across more electricity use, and its warning is that the result holds only while supply keeps pace.

Source: [Watten, Bistline and Blanford, "Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States," arXiv, June 18, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19777).

title: Intel's XBM Patent, Reality-Checked
description: A new Intel filing describes stacked DRAM with no interposer, serial UCIe links, and transistors in the metal layers. Checked against what ships in 2026, it is a worse bet than commodity HBM, and Intel has lost this exact bet before.
content:
On July 2 the US patent office published Intel application US20260191095A1, "Ultra High Bandwidth Memory with Backend Transistors," filed back in December 2024. The coverage settled on calling it XBM, and the framing writes itself: Intel has a plan to kill HBM, the most expensive and most supply-constrained component in the AI buildout. Tom's Hardware, Igor's Lab, and TrendForce all ran it within the week.

My read, after checking the filing coverage against what actually ships in 2026: as a bet, XBM is worse than plain commodity HBM today, and it is not close. The engineering is the interesting part. The timeline and the business model are the problem.

## What the patent actually describes

Three moves, each real:

1. The DRAM cell keeps the standard one-transistor, one-capacitor design, but the access transistors move into the back end of line, the metal and via layers above the silicon. That frees cell area and allows far more vertical connections through the stack.
2. The wide parallel interface goes away. HBM4 talks over a 2,048-bit parallel bus; XBM would serialize memory traffic into UCIe chiplet links running up to 32 GT/s, the top of the current UCIe spec.
3. Because the connection is a normal chiplet link, the silicon interposer goes away too. The stack sits on the package like any other chiplet, in roughly an HBM4 footprint, with built-in self repair. TrendForce's read of the filing has 8-high stacks carrying 96 data blocks, 16-high carrying 192, and sub-channels clocked at 2 GHz.

The target is the right one. On a modern accelerator the HBM stack is widely estimated to be the largest single line on the bill of materials, ahead of the compute die itself, and the advanced packaging that connects it has been a binding constraint on GPU supply since 2023. If you were going to attack one cost in AI hardware, you would attack this one.

One housekeeping note, because the two keep getting mixed up: XBM is not the memory project Intel runs with SAIMEMORY, the SoftBank-backed venture. That one is called ZAM, it attacks stacking and bonding rather than the cell and the interface, and it carries a 2029 target. XBM is a solo Intel filing with no partner and no date.

## A patent is not a product

Intel files thousands of patents a year. This one published on the ordinary 18-month schedule, which means July 2 tells us the clock ran out on the application, and nothing else. There is no test chip, no announced customer, and no roadmap slot. TrendForce, the least excitable outlet that covered it, puts plausible commercialization after 2030.

Hold that date. It is the whole argument.

## The target is moving at full speed

HBM4 went into mass production in February 2026. Samsung and SK hynix, who together produce roughly 90% of the world's HBM, are shipping it now, and Samsung has pushed pin speeds past 11 Gbps against a 2,048-bit interface. Micron ramps its own HBM4 this year with HBM4E on the roadmap for 2027 to 2028. Industry forecasts have the HBM market growing 58% this year to about $54.6 billion. NVIDIA's next platform is designed around HBM4, and every serious accelerator, including the hyperscalers' in-house chips, is an HBM design.

So run the honest comparison: a first-generation exotic memory arriving after 2030 by the friendliest estimate, against the HBM4E or HBM5 of that year, built by three suppliers who have spent a decade fighting each other on yield and price. Nobody's first silicon wins that fight on cost, and cost is the only axis XBM claims.

## The interposer is dying anyway

The expense XBM aims at is already being engineered out inside the HBM ecosystem, on shipping products. TSMC's CoWoS-L replaced the full silicon interposer with an organic substrate and small silicon bridge dies. SK hynix builds HBM4 base dies on TSMC logic processes, which is the same put-logic-under-the-memory idea by another route. The suppliers have spent years on fan-out packaging and standard chiplets. And UCIe is an open standard that Intel co-founded in 2022 and donated the initial spec for, which means the one genuinely novel interface idea here, memory over UCIe, is equally available to the three companies that already run DRAM fabs.

That last point is the structural problem. Intel has not manufactured DRAM since 1985. It invented the commercial DRAM business with the 1103 in 1970 and exited when the business became a commodity knife fight. Somebody has to build XBM's exotic back-end-of-line cells at scale, at DRAM prices, and it is not obvious who. The companies with working DRAM fabs are the ones the patent is aimed at.

## Intel has run this play before

The last time Intel decided the memory hierarchy was broken and only Intel could fix it, the result was Optane. 3D XPoint was announced in 2015 with claims of a thousand times NAND's speed. It was real technology. It shipped, and it worked roughly as described. It still died in July 2022, with a reported $559 million inventory writedown on the way out, because it was a single-supplier memory that required Intel platforms, never got second sources, and could not price against commodity DRAM and NAND made by the exabyte. Micron, the co-developer, walked away first and sold the fab. In the same era Intel sold its NAND business to SK hynix.

Every structural force that killed Optane is lined up against XBM: a single supplier selling against a commodity, and economics that only close if Intel's own platforms win sockets first.

## The physics is not settled either

Set the business aside and the technical questions stay open. Transistors built in back-end metal layers are deposited at low temperature, thin-film style, and nobody has demonstrated DRAM-grade retention and yield from them at density. Serializing memory traffic through UCIe trades HBM's short, wide, slow wires for fast narrow ones, and that trade costs latency and energy per bit, which is the reason HBM was designed wide and slow in the first place. Igor's Lab put it plainly: whether this architecture can compete with HBM4 or HBM4E on bandwidth, power efficiency, latency, and yield remains open. Those are all of the axes that matter.

## Why I am still glad it exists

None of this is rooting against it. The HBM premium sits inside every AI number you look at, including ours: every dollar per GPU-hour on the [GPU Prices](/neocloud-intel) board carries it, and the training-run costs on the Economics tab are, in meaningful part, memory costs with a margin on top. A credible attack on that cost is good for the whole buildout. Intel Foundry also has a rational reason to keep filing these: it sells advanced packaging, and owning memory architectures that showcase it makes sense even if no Intel-branded memory ever ships. If ideas from this filing reach production, my guess is they arrive as foundry packaging IP or folded into a future JEDEC standard, the way Intel donated UCIe.

What I am actually watching: whether ZAM, the Intel project that has a partner and a 2029 target, shows real silicon results; whether an XBM test chip ever surfaces; Micron's HBM4 ramp this year; and how far the incumbents get with custom HBM4E base dies, which is the establishment absorbing XBM's best idea on its own schedule. The equity side lives on [the Stack](/stack). [Micron](/stock/MU) is the US-listed way to own the HBM trade. [Intel](/stock/INTC), for now, has a patent.

title: Tracking the Compute Frontier: Every Named AI Supercluster We Can Verify
description: GridTilt now tracks 235 named AI superclusters by GPUs, chips, and power, and ties each one to the nuclear deals that feed it. Sourced figures are separated from labeled estimates.
content:
GridTilt has a new module: Compute Frontier. It tracks the individual hyperscale clusters the AI race is actually run on, and ties each one to the power that runs it.

## What it tracks

The other GridTilt modules cover the buildout at the level of campuses (the [Power Map](/power-map)), the grid (the [Backlog](/queue)), and equities (the [Stack](/stack)). Compute Frontier adds the compute layer. For each named cluster we record the operator, the status (operational, under construction, or announced), the location and grid region, the chip type, the accelerator count where it has been disclosed, the power rated today and planned at full build-out, the energy source, and the nuclear deal that feeds it where one applies.

The registry now tracks 235 clusters across 77 operators: OpenAI and Oracle's Stargate sites, xAI's Colossus, Meta's Prometheus, Hyperion, and new Texas megacampuses, Microsoft's Fairwater and Pecos sites, Amazon and Anthropic's Project Rainier, Google's TPU campuses, plus CoreWeave, Crusoe, Tesla, Nebius, QTS, and the neocloud and miner-turned-AI operators we added on a June 2026 research pass: Nscale, IREN, Galaxy Digital, Applied Digital, TeraWulf, Cipher Mining, and Stack Infrastructure. Together they add up to about 125 GW of planned power, of which roughly 11 GW is operational today.

## Sourced versus estimated

Data integrity is the point of this project, so the module is explicit about what is known and what is not. Every figure that is a GridTilt estimate, or an announced target that has not been built yet, carries an est. tag in the table. The larger clusters were checked against multiple public sources, including company press releases, Reuters, Tom's Hardware, Data Center Dynamics, SemiAnalysis, and utility filings. Each cluster lists its own source links.

Two rules keep the numbers honest. First, GPU counts appear only where an operator has actually disclosed one. Where a count has not been published, the field reads as not disclosed rather than a guess. Twelve clusters disclose counts today, adding up to about 1.58 million accelerators. Second, power is reported in megawatts at the precision the source gives, with no invented decimals.

## Power needed versus power secured

The reason to put compute and power in one view is to ask a plain question: is the power these clusters need actually secured? Most clusters run on the grid or on-site gas, not on a tracked nuclear deal, and the module says so. A few are different. AWS Susquehanna draws behind-the-meter power from the Susquehanna nuclear plant under the signed Talen agreement. Meta's Pike County campus is tied to the proposed Oklo arrangement. Google's Clarksville site sits in the footprint of the proposed Kairos small modular reactor. Those links point straight to the deals on the Backlog page, so the contract and the compute sit side by side.

## How concentrated is it

The module also measures concentration, because a buildout controlled by a few operators is a different story than a distributed one. On the current data Meta leads the planned buildout, carried mostly by the 5 GW Hyperion campus in Louisiana.

## What is next

The registry is tracked, not exhaustive, and it will grow as new clusters are announced and as estimated figures get replaced by disclosed ones. If you spot a cluster we are missing or a number we should update, the source links make it easy to check the work.

Compute Frontier is live now. See it at [/compute-frontier](/compute-frontier).

title: How Much Power Do AI Data Centers Actually Need?
description: AI data centers consume 288 TWh per year, about 6.4% of US grid capacity. New AI capacity could reach 50 GW by 2030.
content:
The answer is somewhere between 35 and 75 GW of new capacity by 2030.

That range matters. At the low end, existing grid infrastructure can absorb it. At the high end, the US needs to build a UK-sized grid in five years.

## Where we are today

US data centers consumed about 288 TWh in 2025. That is roughly 6.4% of total grid capacity, up from under 3% in 2022. The increase is driven by AI training and inference workloads.

A single H100 GPU consumes about 700W under load. A modern training rack runs 40-80 kW. An AI data center campus draws 100-500 MW.

## The variance drivers

The 35-75 GW range depends on three variables:

**GPU power density**: Blackwell Ultra racks draw 120 kW, nearly double the prior generation. Per-rack power demand keeps climbing.

**Hyperscaler capex execution**: The Big Four committed $328B in combined 2025 capex. If 60% translates to facilities, power demand steepens.

**Grid interconnection speed**: The average PJM queue-to-energize timeline is 4+ years. New generation cannot come online faster than the grid connects it.

## What this means for investors

You cannot download a power plant or 3D-print a transformer. Companies that build and operate power infrastructure face a multi-year demand cycle with no software shortcut.

title: Nuclear Energy and AI Data Centers: Why It Matters
description: Nuclear power provides 24/7 baseload electricity for AI data centers. Three Mile Island restart, Meta's 6.6 GW RFP, and SMR development.
content:
AI data centers need reliable, 24/7 power above all else. Solar and wind are intermittent. Natural gas has carbon and price volatility concerns.

Nuclear is the only proven carbon-free baseload source at scale.

## The baseload argument

A 100,000-GPU training run costs millions per day. If power drops for seconds, the run may need to restart. Intermittent renewables cannot serve as the primary source for large AI facilities.

Nuclear reactors operate at 90%+ capacity factors. They run continuously for 18-24 months between refueling. No other source matches this reliability.

## The restart wave

Microsoft contracted with Constellation Energy to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (835 MW). The plant targets 2028 return to service for Azure data centers.

Meta issued a 6.6 GW nuclear RFP, the largest corporate nuclear procurement. Fulfillment would require restarting retired plants or securing existing output.

## Key stocks

**Constellation Energy (CEG)**: Largest US nuclear fleet with 13 plants. TMI restart and Meta contract make CEG central to the nuclear-AI thesis.

**Vistra Corp (VST)**: 41 GW generation capacity including Comanche Peak nuclear. Strong merchant power exposure from rising wholesale prices.

**Cameco (CCJ)**: Largest Western uranium producer. Cigar Lake mine produces about 18M lbs of U3O8 per year.

**Oklo (OKLO)**: Building 15 MW Aurora microreactors. NRC approval would certify the first commercial fast spectrum reactor.

title: The PJM Interconnection Queue: AI's Biggest Bottleneck
description: PJM's interconnection queue has 4+ year wait times and 250 GW pending. This bottleneck limits how fast AI data center power comes online.
content:
PJM manages the largest US electricity market. It serves 65 million customers across 13 states. It also hosts Data Center Alley in Northern Virginia.

The bottleneck is the interconnection queue.

## What the queue is

Any new generation source or large load must pass an interconnection study. PJM checks whether the grid can handle the connection without reliability issues.

As of early 2026, PJM's queue holds over 250 GW of requests. Average time from application to energization is 4+ years. Some projects have waited 6-7 years.

## Why it matters for AI

Every new data center needs grid power. Every nuclear restart needs grid connection. The queue is the biggest constraint on AI power infrastructure buildout speed.

PJM's 2025/2026 capacity auction cleared at $270/MW-day, a record. Clearing prices signal that supply is not keeping up with demand.

## FERC Order 1920

FERC Order 1920 mandates long-range transmission planning. Regional utilities must file 20-year expansion plans that account for AI data center load growth. The first filing deadline is July 2026.

## The investment implication

The queue creates a natural moat for existing generators. If new supply takes 4+ years, companies that own operating plants (CEG, VST, NRG) benefit from scarcity pricing.

title: The Transformer Shortage That Could Slow AI
description: The US produces about 60 large power transformers per year. AI demand could require 80-150+ annually. Lead times exceed 4 years.
content:
A large power transformer (LPT) sits between every power plant and data center. It weighs 200-400 tons and takes 12-18 months to build.

Each one costs $5-15M. There are not enough of them.

## The math

The US has about 2,000 LPTs in service. Domestic production is roughly 60 per year. The fleet averages 40+ years old, so replacement demand alone consumes much of production.

Now add AI data centers. GridTilt estimates the base case (50 GW by 2030) needs 80-100 additional LPTs per year. The aggressive case (75 GW) needs 150+.

Domestic supply cannot meet that. Importing is difficult because LPTs are custom-engineered.

## Who benefits

**GE Vernova (GEV)**: Manufactures transformers and grid equipment. Backlog at record levels with 4+ year lead times.

**Eaton (ETN)**: Switchgear and power distribution units. Datacenter order intake is their key earnings metric.

**Hubbell (HUBB)**: Utility electrical equipment. Elevated demand from grid modernization and data center construction.

## The constraint timeline

This shortage is not temporary. New factories need specialized tooling, trained workers, and 2-3 years to build. Demand will exceed supply for multiple years.

title: Uranium Stocks and AI: The Supply Chain Connection
description: Nuclear restarts from AI demand create new uranium fuel requirements. Western supply is constrained with 40% Kazakh import dependency.
content:
Every nuclear reactor consumes enriched uranium fuel. Every restart creates new fuel demand. AI data centers are driving the largest nuclear procurement wave in decades.

## The fuel cycle

Uranium goes through four steps before reaching a reactor:

1. **Mining**: Extracting U3O8 (yellowcake)
2. **Conversion**: Converting to UF6 gas
3. **Enrichment**: Raising U-235 from 0.7% to 3-5%
4. **Fabrication**: Building fuel assemblies

Each step has its own supply chain and bottlenecks. Total timeline: 18-24 months from mine to reactor.

## Supply constraints

Global production has been below consumption since 2016. Inventory drawdowns and recycled material filled the gap. Those secondary sources are depleting.

The US imports about 40% of its uranium from Kazakhstan. Sanctions or production disruptions could tighten supply fast. Spot prices hit about $92/lb in March 2026, up from $50/lb in 2023.

## Key miners

**Cameco (CCJ)**: Largest Western producer. Cigar Lake produces 18M lbs/year. Strong long-term contract book.

**NexGen Energy (NXE)**: Developing Rook I in Saskatchewan's Athabasca Basin. One of the highest-grade undeveloped deposits globally.

**Uranium Energy Corp (UEC)**: US-focused with ISR operations in Wyoming and Texas. Benefits from domestic procurement preferences.

title: Behind-the-Meter Power: Why Hyperscalers Are Building Their Own Plants
description: Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft contract directly with generators, bypassing the grid. This behind-the-meter strategy reshapes utility economics.
content:
The grid queue is 4+ years. Wholesale prices are rising. Renewables cannot support 24/7 AI training.

Hyperscalers are building their own power.

## What behind-the-meter means

Behind-the-meter (BTM) places a generator at the point of consumption. The data center connects directly to a dedicated power plant, bypassing the grid.

Industrial facilities have used cogeneration for decades. What is new is the scale. Hyperscalers are signing multi-hundred-megawatt BTM agreements that did not exist five years ago.

## The deals

**Microsoft + Constellation**: TMI Unit 1 restart (835 MW) under a 20-year PPA. Nuclear baseload delivered directly to Azure operations.

**Amazon + Talen Energy**: Data center campus adjacent to Susquehanna nuclear plant. BTM arrangement provides up to 960 MW.

**Meta's 6.6 GW RFP**: The largest corporate nuclear procurement. Winning bids could include BTM and traditional PPAs.

**xAI Memphis Colossus**: On-site gas turbines power 100,000+ GPUs while awaiting grid interconnection.

## What it means for utilities

BTM bypasses transmission and distribution charges. This creates regulatory tension. Utilities like Dominion and PPL are creating specialized data center tariffs in response.

## The investor angle

BTM favors companies owning generation near data center sites. CEG and VST are best-positioned in nuclear. GEV benefits from gas turbine sales.
